## General Tijdeman–Wang dependency graph

```text
Schmidt–Schlickewei Subspace Theorem (rational places)
  → nondegenerate projective S-unit finiteness
    [EGST88 Theorem 1 / Corollary 1.1; TiWa88 Lemma 6]
  → finite normalized minimal zero-sum templates, lengths 2–6
  → finite partitions of equality of two three-term representations
  → finitely many collapsed coefficients; enlarge finitely generated group
  → strong induction for positive sums of at most three weighted S-units
    [TiWa88 Theorem 6 → Theorem 5]
  → uniform bound for summand multisets representing n
  → raw exponent-tuple bound [Counting.lean: factor 6]
  → jsp_000334 : NewmanConjecture
  → principal build / axiom audit / clean committed reproduction
  → independent source, statement and proof review
```

In this general Theorem 6 graph, all source theorem nodes remain unproved except the counting bridge. Positivity rules out vanishing subsums within either original representation, but not within the signed difference of two representations. Equal terms and repeated summands must remain covered. Partitions with singleton terms on each side correspond to the same multiset; every genuinely distinct pair has a collapse reducing arity. Finite coefficients can introduce primes outside `{2,3}`; restricting the deep input to the original two generators would not justify the general induction. The group must be enlarged by finitely many coefficients, preserving finite generation.

For the general Tijdeman–Wang alternative, the deepest obligation is `ProjectiveSUnitFiniteness` in `Spike.lean`: for every finitely generated subgroup of rational units, nondegenerate zero-sum vectors of lengths 2–6 normalized to first coordinate 1 form a finite set. The proposition is a specification, not an axiom and not a proved theorem. It is qualitative and supplies no uniform coefficient bound by itself. For that general alternative, uniformity in `n` would be produced by the partition/induction argument, which is not implemented. For the selected specialized route, M3.2 now proves the complete fixed-reference implication described below.

## Foundational correction pass: exact algebraic and analytic boundary

The bounded three-term finiteness step now compiles in the pinned environment. `ThreeTermHyperplaneCover G` says that one finite set of nonzero rational coefficient pairs covers the first two coordinates of every vector in `normalizedRelations G 2`. `normalized_three_term_finite_of_hyperplane_cover` proves that these normalized relations are finite: if `p₀ x₀ + p₁ x₁ = 0` and `x₀ = 1`, then `p₁ ≠ 0`, `x₁ = -p₀/p₁` and `x₂ = p₀/p₁ - 1`. The possible triples are a subset of the image of the finite coefficient set. This is the three-term specialization of EGST88's Subspace-Theorem reduction, printed pp. 123–124, and hence a finiteness step beyond normalization. It uses no S-unit analytic assumption implicitly.

`three_term_hyperplane_cover_iff_finite` proves the converse too. Consequently the new cover specification is exactly as hard as normalized three-term finiteness; introducing it has not removed or proved the analytic difficulty. For any finite rational-unit generator set `F`, the next exact Lean goal is:

```lean
ThreeTermHyperplaneCover (Subgroup.closure (F : Set ℚˣ))
```

It remains unproved even for the subgroup generated by `-1`, `2`, `3`. `ProjectiveSUnitFiniteness` remains unproved for `m = 2, 3, 4, 5`. No inference from a conditional finiteness theorem to an unconditional theorem is authorized.

The missing analytic chain is explicit: choose the finite prime support of the rational generators, add the infinite place; prove the rational product formula and homogeneous height invariance; for each place omit a maximal coordinate from the coordinate-and-sum family; prove the remaining forms nonsingular and the required height-decaying product inequality; apply a proved rational finite-place Subspace Theorem to obtain a finite proper cover of the first `m` coordinates. EGST88 (4.5)–(4.6), p. 123, supplies this source construction. At `m = 2` the new theorem finishes the argument. At `m = 3..5`, p. 124 requires a second induction: select a minimal vanishing block for each additional hyperplane relation, apply lower-arity weighted S-unit finiteness to its coefficient-weighted coordinates, collapse that block in the original relation, show the collapsed coefficient nonzero using original nondegeneracy, apply lower-arity finiteness again, and reconstruct. This requires finiteness for arbitrary fixed nonzero rational coefficients, not just all coefficients equal to 1. None of those analytic or higher-arity induction steps is implemented yet.

A smaller uniform-count bridge is mathematically available for the positive fixed-arity target. Compare each representation with one fixed representation of the same `n`. For each of its three labeled summands, take a minimal zero block containing that summand in the signed six-term difference. Such a block exists: choose a smallest zero subset containing the chosen index; a zero proper subblock either contains that index or can be removed, contradicting minimality. Positivity forces an opposite-sign summand in the block. Projective finiteness through six terms gives a finite set `R` of unsigned ratios inside such blocks. Each labeled summand is `q` times one of the three fixed summands, with `q ∈ R`. Injectivity of labeled summands therefore embeds all exponent tuples into `(Fin 3 × R)^3`, giving a bound `(3 * |R|)^3` independent of `n`. Empty solution sets have count zero; repeated summands and multiple codes cause no difficulty because a code is chosen once per representation and its injectivity follows from the represented numerical values. This argument is a specialized consequence of Tijdeman–Wang Lemma 6 and positivity, not a claim that it is the published proof of their general Theorem 6.

This fixed-reference idea was identified during static inspection of plby's `EGST.lean` at commit `8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e` and must be attributed if used. No code was copied or imported. It removes the need for finite coefficient enlargement and uniform induction **in the final positive Newman counting bridge**. Those nodes remain mandatory if the general Tijdeman–Wang Theorem 6 route above is chosen. Weighted-coefficient induction inside S-unit finiteness itself is still required. The specialized route needs only the fixed group generated by `-1`, `2`, `3`, and rational three-place Subspace-Theorem forms in dimensions 2–5; the stronger `ProjectiveSUnitFiniteness` specification for every finitely generated rational subgroup remains available but is no longer claimed to be logically necessary for the narrower target. The approved principal statement and counting lemmas are unchanged.

## M3.4 — exact Subspace application bridge complete

`SubspaceBridge.lean` supplies the complete application boundary. `integralPair q = [q.den, q.num]` is nonzero and Bézout-primitive for every rational `q`, without a sign assumption on its numerator. For `q=x₁` in the fixed group, `sunit_den_prime_support` proves every prime dividing the denominator is 2 or 3, using outside-prime norm identity and numerator/denominator coprimality; factorization then constructs the denominator as an actual member of `fixedSUnitGroup`. `exists_primitive_sunit_pair` proves projective scaling by that member and exact equality of normalized pair height with the primitive pair's Archimedean sup height. `primitive_pair_local_height` proves finite-place sup norm 1 at every prime from Bézout, so no residual finite-place height factor is assumed.

`choiceFormsProduct` retains different coordinate-plus-sum form pairs at the three places. `choice_forms_independent` discharges nonsingularity for every pattern. `choiceFormsProduct_sunit_scale` proves exact unnormalized product invariance under the constructed S-unit scale; `choiceFormsProduct_retained` identifies the selected smaller-coordinate product. `exists_primitive_strong_pair` uses `three_term_normalized_product_height` and the positive/nonzero height to prove the exact equality `choiceFormsProduct choice z * archPairHeight z = 1`. It supplies all primitive, scaling, height and strong-inequality evidence together. Nonsingularity and product transfer hold for every pattern; the strong equality holds for the locally selected smaller-coordinate pattern, exactly as in EGST. Requiring the strong inequality for every arbitrary pattern would be false (the constant second-coordinate pattern on the primitive pair `(4,-3)` gives product times height 4). No positivity of the second coordinate is needed.

The previously displayed dimension-two theorem is now represented exactly by `ThreePlaceSubspaceCover : Prop`. It remains unproved and is not an axiom. Its full definition is printed in Audit: for each `choice : Fin 3 → Fin 2`, finitely many nonzero rational coefficient vectors cover every Bézout-primitive integer pair satisfying the original strong inequality with right side 1. The definition has no extra arithmetic assumption. The completed declarations are:

```lean
theorem three_term_cover_of_subspace (hST : ThreePlaceSubspaceCover) :
  ThreeTermHyperplaneCover fixedSUnitGroup

theorem three_term_finite_of_subspace (hST : ThreePlaceSubspaceCover) :
  (normalizedRelations fixedSUnitGroup 2).Finite
```

### Exact statements and rational specialization

Schlickewei Satz 2.1, printed p.153, assumes n≥2, distinct primes, an independent algebraic-coefficient basis of forms at each real/p-adic place, fixed real exponents with total sum zero and nonpositive finite-place exponents, an unbounded set of real Q>1, and a fixed δ>0 and 1≤d≤n−1 with λ_d(Q)<λ_(d+1)(Q)Q^(−δ). Here Π(Q) is the real parallelepiped (2.3), G(Q) is the integer congruence lattice (2.4), and the λ_i are its successive minima. The conclusion is a fixed rational d-dimensional subspace containing vectors attaining the first d minima on an unbounded subset of Q. This is a subsequence stabilization theorem, not itself a finite cover or a statement about weak-general Roth systems. The latter criterion is Satz 1.2, proved separately in §7 using Satz 2.1. Accordingly the M3.10 proposed next milestone's identification of a Roth-system criterion with Satz 2.1 is refined here.

For our application take n=3, t=2, primes 2 and 3, and d=1 or 2. The three coordinate/sum matrices are integral unimodular, with determinants respectively 1, −1, 1; sign normalization leaves every place norm unchanged. No algebraic field extension is required, and rational coefficient-height estimates replace the general algebraic norm estimates with degree D=1. Neither distinctness of coordinates nor pairwise coprimality is introduced. Uniformly bounded exponent systems can be rescaled by replacing Q with a fixed positive power of Q; §6 explicitly permits bounded compound exponents rather than requiring their unit bound literally.

### Interaction of the three places and eventual cover

The finite places define the changing integer lattice; the real place defines the changing body. Integer floor exponents approximate the Q-power 2/3 bounds with constants depending only on the fixed primes. Their joint determinant is a product of powers of 2 and 3, and total exponent zero makes volume/covolume uniformly normalized. Both finite places participate independently in the reciprocal lattice and compound construction. In Lemma 4.1 the cofactor inequalities are multiplied across all three places; dividing by the primitive cofactor's gcd is legitimate because an integer W has |W|·|W|₂·|W|₃≥1, without assuming W is an S-unit. Rational nonzero cofactor evaluations have an Archimedean integer lower bound and finite-place inverse-height lower bounds. These force the primitive normal's height to grow, supplying the missing polynomial/Roth contradiction rather than eliminating it.

For the endpoint, zero form values lie in their finitely many kernels. At large height H, a nonzero integral coordinate/sum value is between 1 and 3H at infinity and between (3H)⁻¹ and 1 at each finite place. Nine logarithmic exponents therefore lie in a fixed bounded interval and have sum at most −1. A finite mesh of width less than 1/18 gives fixed upper exponents of total sum at most −1/2. Add the same positive correction to the three real exponents to make their total with the six finite exponents zero. The original vectors then lie in a uniformly shrinking real body within the same 2/3 lattice. A successive-minima product bound supplies a persistent gap with d=1 or 2 above the size of these vectors; Satz 2.1 concentrates an unbounded subsequence in a proper rational subspace. The gap must be chosen so that the original points themselves, not only some unrelated short lattice vectors, lie in the low-minimum span. Schmidt's Lemma 6 general-position sequence contradiction upgrades this concentration to finite coverage for each exponent pattern. A finite union handles exponent patterns, 27 form choices, zero kernels and bounded-height exceptions. This is an unformalized reconstruction whose deep premises remain open; it is not a claim that possessing Satz 2.1's statement completes the cover.
